items.title: Coming From Sherman Oaks for a Haircut
items.content_text: A barbershop near Sherman Oaks does not have to be in Sherman Oaks. Amir Precision Cuts is a short hop west along Ventura Boulevard, at 17388 in Encino. For most men on the Sherman Oaks side the drive is under ten minutes, and it buys a single-barber chair instead of whoever is free. Ventura Boulevard is the whole route. It runs continuously from Sherman Oaks into Encino, so there is no clever way to do it and no reason to look for one. You stay on the boulevard, you pass Hayvenhurst Avenue, and the shop is between there and Louise Avenue. Traffic is the only variable worth planning around, and it behaves predictably. Late morning and early afternoon are clear. The stretch tightens up between about four and six in the evening, which is the window men most want, so a 7pm slot on a weekday is often a faster trip than a 5pm one even though it feels later. Tuesday to Friday the shop is open until 8, which makes that a real option rather than a theoretical one. Coming from the eastern end of Sherman Oaks, near the 405, allow fifteen minutes at rush hour and eight otherwise. From the middle of Sherman Oaks it is less. Nobody is asking you to cross the Valley. This is one neighbourhood over. In practice that makes it an Encino barber for Sherman Oaks men as much as for Encino ones. Most men in Sherman Oaks already have a haircut option closer than this one. Usually several. The question is not whether a closer chair exists — it is what the closer chair does differently, and the honest answer has nothing to do with skill and everything to do with structure. At a shop with a rota, you book a haircut. You do not book a person. Whoever is free takes you, and the man who cut your hair well in March is not necessarily the man who cuts it in July. That means the growth pattern conversation resets every visit. Your cowlick gets rediscovered. The neckline decision gets made again, sometimes differently, and a neckline that has been blocked once and tapered the next time never quite settles. Here there is one barber. Amir cuts every appointment, and the chair is not double-booked, which changes two things. The first is continuity: the second visit starts where the first one ended rather than at the beginning. The second is pace — nobody is being started in your slot, so the last five minutes of the cut are not being borrowed from someone else's first five. > "The second haircut is where a client finds out whether it was luck. If it is the same hands, it is not luck." > — Amir, barber None of that is an argument against the shop down the street from you. It is a description of a trade: a few more minutes in the car for a chair that remembers what your hair does. This barbershop near Sherman Oaks runs appointment-only, so the drive is never wasted on a queue. That is the main practical point for anyone travelling in from the Sherman Oaks side — you are not gambling twelve minutes of Ventura Boulevard on whether there is a seat. A haircut runs about forty-five minutes. A haircut and beard trim together is $70 and takes about an hour and a quarter, and it is the appointment most men who drive in choose, because the two lines get shaped to work with each other in one visit rather than in two. If you are making a trip out of it anyway, doing both is the version that respects the trip. Hours are Tuesday to Friday, 9 until 8, and Saturday 9 until 7. Closed Sunday and Monday. Saturday fills before the weekdays do, so if you want a Saturday morning slot, ask earlier in the week. Directions and hours are on the site, along with parking notes. Speaking of which: street parking along Ventura Boulevard, metered on the closest blocks. Midweek it is easy. Saturday takes a few extra minutes. If you are driving in from Sherman Oaks on a Saturday, the parking is more likely to cost you time than the drive is. That depends on something specific: how your last three haircuts compared to each other. If they were the same cut three times, whatever you are doing is working, and there is no argument here worth reading. If they were three variations — one good, one flat, one where the back was suddenly higher than you wanted — then the inconsistency is structural rather than bad luck, and driving ten minutes west along the boulevard is a cheap way to fix a structural problem. Men from Sherman Oaks, Van Nuys and Studio City come in for that reason more than any other. Not because Encino has better barbers — there is no argument being made about neighbourhoods here. Because one chair produces one result, and three visits to one chair produce three versions of the same haircut rather than three different haircuts. Consistency is an unglamorous thing to drive ten minutes for, and it is also the only thing most men actually want from a barber once they have found a shape that suits them. The rest of the practical detail is in the common questions.

items.title: Men's Haircuts in Encino: What $50 Actually Buys
items.content_text: A men's haircut in Encino is $50 at Amir Precision Cuts. That covers the consultation, the cut itself shaped to how your hair grows, and the neckline and edges finished by hand at the end. It is one price rather than a starting point, and it is the same on a Tuesday as it is on a Saturday. Price pages tend to describe a haircut with adjectives. Here is the itemised version instead. **The consultation.** Three or four minutes at the start, standing, before anything is cut. You say what you want. Amir looks at how the hair is actually behaving that day — where the crown sits, which way the back grows, whether the hairline at the temple is holding a line or receding past one. If what you asked for will not sit the way you are picturing, that is when you find out, not three weeks later. **The cut.** Clipper work, scissor work, or both, depending on what the shape needs. There is no menu distinction between them at this price, because deciding which one a head wants is part of the job rather than an upgrade. **The neckline and the edges.** The last part, and the part that determines how the cut looks in week three. A blocked neckline on hair that grows downward will look untidy long before the length does. A taper on the same head will not. This decision is made deliberately, once, with your growth pattern in front of the barber rather than a house style. **The finish.** The cut checked in daylight from more than one angle, with a comb rather than product, so what you see in the mirror is the cut and not a styling job on top of it. What $50 does not include is a beard. A beard trim in Encino on its own is $40, and the two together are $70 — cheaper than paying twice, and better, because the beard line and the neckline get shaped to agree with each other in one sitting. Plenty of shops quote a men's haircut in Encino "from" a number. That phrasing exists for a reason, and the reason is rarely in the client's favour: it lets the number in the search result be lower than the number at the till. The price here is $50 because that is what it costs. Length does not change it. Difficulty does not change it. A man with thick hair that needs forty minutes of scissor work over the top pays the same as a man who wants a skin fade and is out in half an hour. Averaging across a week is easier for everyone than negotiating at the mirror. The exception is genuinely different work rather than a harder version of the same work. A hot towel shave is its own appointment at $60. Scissor work over the whole head with the beard shaped to match is $90 and takes an hour and a half. Those are not surcharges on a haircut; they are different services with their own time. > "If I quoted from a price I would be guessing at the end of every appointment. One number means the only thing we discuss in the chair is the hair." > — Amir, barber A haircut is priced in minutes more honestly than it is priced in skill, and $50 buys about forty-five of them. That is enough time to cut wet and check dry. Hair lies differently once it dries, particularly at the crown and around a cowlick, and a shape that looked balanced wet can sit two millimetres off once the water leaves it. Forty-five minutes leaves room to go back in. Twenty-five does not. It is also enough time to do the neckline once, properly, rather than quickly and then again. And it is enough to say at the end when you should come back — which for most men here is a few weeks longer than they expect, because a cut shaped to a growth pattern grows out into a shape rather than out of one. Where that time goes is the difference between a cheap cut and a cut that holds. It is not mystique. It is minutes, and minutes are the one input a barber cannot fake. It is worth saying what forty-five minutes does not buy, because the honest version of a price page has a limit in it. It does not buy a different head of hair. A crown that sits forward will still sit forward. A hairline that has moved back will not come forward because the cut around it is precise. What the time buys is a shape that works with those facts instead of against them, and a barber who tells you which is which before the clippers come out rather than after. The shop is on Ventura Boulevard in Encino, 91316, between Louise Avenue and Hayvenhurst Avenue. If you are looking for a barber in Encino, CA rather than a chain further along the boulevard, that is the address. Full details of our location are on the site. It runs by appointment only — one barber, one chair, not double-booked — Tuesday to Friday until 8 in the evening and Saturday until 7. Closed Sunday and Monday. Midweek slots are usually available a day or two out. Saturday fills first, so book it earlier in the week if that is the day you need. Men coming from Sherman Oaks, Tarzana or Van Nuys tend to take a weekday evening for exactly that reason. items.title: For Men in Tarzana and Reseda: Worth the Ten Minutes
items.content_text: A barber near Tarzana is usually a barber in Tarzana. This one is ten minutes east, on Ventura Boulevard in Encino, and the reason men make that drive is time rather than distance: an appointment that starts when it says it does, and finishes without being hurried into the next one. From central Tarzana it is about ten minutes east along Ventura Boulevard. From the Reseda side, coming down Hayvenhurst Avenue or Louise Avenue, closer to twelve. From Lake Balboa, allow fifteen. None of that is a long way by Valley standards — it is the sort of trip most men already make for a supermarket they prefer. The part worth planning is the hour, not the mileage. Ventura Boulevard eastbound is clear before eleven and after seven, and slow from about four. A 9am appointment and a 7pm appointment both get you a fast run in each direction; a 5pm one taxes you twice. Tuesday through Friday the shop is open until 8, which makes the late slot a real choice rather than a theoretical one, and Saturday closes at 7. If you are coming from the Reseda area or from anywhere near the Sepulveda Basin Recreation Area, the practical move is to attach the appointment to something you were already going to do on this stretch. Encino Park and Los Encinos State Historic Park are minutes away. Men who fold the cut into a run of errands stop thinking about the drive at all. If you are looking for a barber near Lake Balboa or the western end of the Basin, that is the framing that makes the distance disappear: it is not a separate journey, it is one more stop on a road you were already on. Because there is nothing to wait for when you arrive. The shop takes appointments only. One barber, one chair. That is a limitation if you are two blocks away and want a cut in twenty minutes, and it is the entire point if you have just driven in from Tarzana — nobody who has spent twelve minutes on the boulevard should then spend twenty-five in a chair by the window watching two men get seen first. It also means the slot is the slot. A shop that runs a queue absorbs its overruns by taking them out of whoever is next. A shop with one chair and a booked diary absorbs them by finishing properly and starting the following appointment a few minutes late, which is a smaller and more honest debt. > "If someone has driven in from Reseda I owe them the whole appointment, not the part that fits before the next man is due." > — Amir, barber Call or message on Instagram a day or two ahead midweek. Saturdays go earlier in the week, and that is the one day where turning up hopeful genuinely does not work. The service most men who drive in choose is the longer one, and it is a sensible instinct. A haircut on its own is $50 and about forty-five minutes. A scissor cut and beard trim is $90 and an hour and a half — scissor work over the whole head for length and movement, with the beard shaped to sit against it. The second one is not a better version of the first; it is different work, and it is the one that changes how a head looks for a month rather than a fortnight. If you are driving fifteen minutes each way, the arithmetic favours the longer appointment. Two thirty-minute visits cost you an hour of Ventura Boulevard between them. One ninety-minute visit costs you the same half hour of driving as a forty-five-minute one, and the result holds longer. Men from the Tarzana and Reseda side book the longer services more often than men who walk in from three blocks away, and that is not a coincidence. A hot towel shave is its own appointment at $60. It is worth booking as a separate visit rather than tacking it on, because the pace is the product and there is no version of it that is quicker. One thing not to do is book the longest service on your first visit. A first appointment is partly a conversation about what your hair actually does, and it is easier to have that conversation over a cut than over ninety minutes of scissor work committed to in advance. Come once for the haircut, see whether the shape holds three weeks later, and book the longer service after that. Driving in twice to find out is a smaller cost than driving in once and paying ninety for a shape you did not want. Two things save the trip. First, come with your hair the way it normally is. Not freshly wet, not flattened under a cap for the whole drive. How it sits when you walk in is the information the cut gets built on, and a cap for fifteen minutes on the 101 hides the crown entirely. Second, know when you last had it cut, roughly. Three weeks and six weeks are different problems, and the answer changes what can be done in one sitting. If you are not sure, say so — a guess presented as a fact is worse than not knowing. Directions and hours are on the site, along with the parking notes. Street parking runs along Ventura Boulevard and is metered on the blocks nearest the shop. Midweek it is easy. The common questions cover the rest.

items.title: A Barber a Short Walk From the Encino Oak Tree
items.content_text: Amir Precision Cuts sits on Ventura Boulevard in Encino, a few minutes on foot from the Encino Oak Tree and just west of Louise Avenue. Anyone already on that stretch — working there, running errands, walking back from Encino Park — can reach the chair without getting into a car. Appointments run Tuesday to Saturday. This barbershop on Ventura Boulevard in Encino sits on a stretch that changes character every few blocks. The shop is at 17388, between Louise Avenue and Hayvenhurst Avenue, on the run where the storefronts sit close together and the sidewalk is wide enough to be worth using. The Encino Oak Tree is a few minutes east. Los Encinos State Historic Park is a little further along in the same direction, and Encino Park sits north of the boulevard. That geography does something to how often men get their hair cut, and it is not a small thing. A barber you can walk to is a barber you actually see. The appointment stops being an errand that needs a parking plan and becomes fifteen minutes of walking either side of the work. Men who live or work between Hayvenhurst and Louise tend to come back on a sensible interval for exactly that reason. Men who have to drive across the Valley tend to stretch it, and a stretched interval is what turns a good cut into a shape that has to be rebuilt. That is the practical case for choosing a barber near the Encino Oak Tree over one you have to plan a trip around. If you are looking for a barber near the Encino Oak Tree, the landmark is the easier way to find the shop. Start at the tree, walk west along the boulevard, and you are there before the walk becomes a journey. More than you would expect. You turn up unhurried. Nobody who has just spent six minutes circling for a space sits down relaxed, and the first two minutes of an appointment are the ones where you explain what you want. Those two minutes decide the cut. Rushing them is how men end up with a shape they did not ask for and cannot describe afterwards. Your hair also arrives in its own state. A car headrest flattens the back and a driver's window pushes one side around. Neither is permanent, but both make it harder to read how the hair actually falls, and how it falls is what the cut has to work with. Hair that has been walked in sits the way it sits at home. Then there is the end of the appointment. A fresh cut goes straight under a seatbelt and a headrest when you drive off, which is a strange way to finish something that was just shaped carefully. Walking out onto the boulevard is a better last five minutes. You see it in daylight, in a window, at the angle other people will see it. None of this is a reason to walk if you live in Tarzana. It is a reason to walk if you already could. Amir works alone. Every appointment is with him, and the chair is not double-booked — that is the whole reason the shop runs on appointments rather than a queue. Nobody is parked in a waiting area while a second client is started in the same time slot. The practical effect is that the shop cannot absorb a man who simply appears at the door. It can nearly always find him a slot a day or two out. Midweek is easier than Saturday. If you want to book on your way past, message on Instagram rather than standing outside working out whether the door is open. > "A man who has walked five minutes to get here talks differently in the first minute than a man who has just parked. I get better information, so he gets a better cut." > — Amir, barber The consultation is not a formality. It is where the neckline gets decided, and the neckline is the part of a haircut that dates first. Most people still drive, and it works. Street parking runs along Ventura Boulevard, metered nearest the shop and free further out as you move away from the busiest blocks. Midweek it is straightforward. Saturday is genuinely busier — the boulevard fills, the closest meters go first, and the walk from wherever you land might be the five minutes you were trying to avoid. Leave a few extra minutes rather than arriving at the appointment already behind it. Metro runs along the boulevard, with stops a short walk either side of Louise Avenue. For men coming from Sherman Oaks or Van Nuys without a car, that is the simplest way in. A walkable barber in Encino only stays walkable if the last part of the journey is short, and from those stops it is. Hours are Tuesday to Friday, 9 in the morning until 8 in the evening, and Saturday until 7. Closed Sunday and Monday. Full directions and hours are on the site, and if something about the visit is unclear, the common questions probably cover it. A haircut in Encino is $50, and the shape of the visit is the same whether you walked or drove. The walk is just a better version of the same appointment.
